entry: American actress and comedian. Leachman won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for *The Last Picture Show* (1971) and eight Primetime Emmy Awards from 22 nominations, including for *The Mary Tyler Moore Show*. She won a Golden Globe for the spinoff *Phyllis*, and was part of [[Mel Brooks]]'s ensemble cast in *Young Frankenstein* (1974). She also wrote her memoir *Cloris: My Autobiography* (2009).

Powered household appliance that removes moisture from washed clothing, bedding and other [[Textile|textiles]]. Tumble dryers rotate clothes in a drum through which heated air is circulated to evaporate moisture, and the humid air is usually vented outside. Condenser dryers instead cool the air with a heat exchanger and collect the condensed water in a drain or tank, so the heat stays in the room and drying takes somewhat longer. [[Heat pump]] dryers dehumidify the air and use under half the energy per load of a condenser dryer. Spin dryers extract water by spinning the drum faster than a [[Washing machine|washer]] can, saving time and energy in large laundry operations such as hospitals. Lint buildup in vents and drums causes fire risk, accounting for approximately 15,000 residential structure fires per year in the United States.

Range of sectors that design, produce and sell clothing, from [[Textile|textile]] mills to apparel retail. Mills turn natural or synthetic fibers into [[Yarn|yarn]], which is woven or knitted into cloth for garments, and the industry also includes embroidery and [[Fashion design|fashion design]]. A 1901 census of Bristol, England, found that female outworkers, who worked from home outside factories, made up nearly one-third of all workers in the clothing industry. Under [[Globalization|globalization]], much manufacturing moved to low-wage countries such as [[Bangladesh]], China and Vietnam, while fashion design, modeling and retail shifted toward centers such as [[London]] and the SoHo district of New York City. The sector employs roughly 60 million factory workers and had annual revenues exceeding US $1.77 trillion in 2024. It provides livelihoods in developing economies, but critics cite low wages and hazardous conditions, exemplified by the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse.

Public sculpture by artist Anish Kapoor in Millennium Park, [[Chicago]]. Constructed between 2004 and 2006, the [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]] sculpture is nicknamed "The Bean" for its shape. Its 168 plates are welded together into a highly polished surface with no visible seams, which reflects and distorts the city's skyline and passing clouds. Kapoor's design was inspired by liquid [[Mercury (element)|mercury]]. Visitors can walk around and under its 12-foot (3.7 m) arch, where a concave chamber called the omphalos multiplies reflections. Cloud Gate was formally dedicated on May 15, 2006.

[[Particle detector]] that makes the paths of [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]] visible. Also called a Wilson chamber, it holds a supersaturated vapor of [[Water|water]] or [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]]. A charged particle knocks electrons off gas molecules, leaving ions that act as condensation centers for a droplet trail visible for several seconds. [[Alpha particle]] tracks are thick and straight, while [[Beta particle|beta particle]] tracks are wispy and deflected. Scottish physicist Charles Thomson Rees Wilson invented the chamber in the early 1900s and received half the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on it. Cloud chambers played a central role in discoveries such as the [[Positron|positron]], found by Carl Anderson in 1932, until bubble chambers largely replaced them in the 1950s. Simplified versions remain common in education.

Model of shared, [[Internet|internet]]-based computing in which scalable resources are available on demand. The International Organization for Standardization defines it as network access to a scalable and elastic pool of shareable physical or virtual resources. In 2011, the National Institute of Standards and Technology identified five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. In Q4 2025, [[Amazon Web Services]] led the global cloud infrastructure market with a 28% share, ahead of Microsoft Azure at 21% and Google Cloud at 14%, according to Synergy Research Group.

American technology company based in [[San Francisco]]. Founded in 2009 by Matthew Prince, Lee Holloway and Michelle Zatlyn, it acts primarily as a reverse proxy between websites and their hosts, providing [[Internet|internet]] security, content delivery network services and DDoS mitigation. It went public on the [[New York Stock Exchange]] in 2019 under the ticker NET. According to W3Techs, it was used by about 21.3% of all websites as of January 2026. Critics argue that its services enable harmful actors, and the company has terminated services for sites including The Daily Stormer, 8chan and Kiwi Farms after significant public pressure.

Aromatic, dried, unopened [[Flower|flower]] bud of the evergreen tree *Syzygium aromaticum*, family [[Myrtaceae]]. Cloves are native to the [[Maluku Islands]] of [[Indonesia]], where the tree grows 8–12 m tall, and buds are harvested at 1.5–2 cm in length. Cloves flavor meats such as baked ham, curries and fruit dishes, and are a common element of [[Spice|spice]] blends such as pumpkin pie spice. Their characteristic taste comes largely from the chemical eugenol. Clove oil is applied to toothaches and used to inhibit mold growth on some foods. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has not approved clove for any medicinal purpose, and oral use may cause adverse effects in people with liver disease, blood-clotting or immune system disorders, or food allergies. Indonesia leads global production, at about 146 thousand metric tons in 2023.

[[Franks|Frankish]] king (r. 481–511), founder of the [[Merovingian dynasty]]. Clovis succeeded his father, Childeric I, as king of the Salian Franks and became the first Frankish king to unite the Franks under a single ruler, so that the kingship passed to his heirs. At the Battle of Soissons (486) he took a rump state of the fragmenting [[Western Roman Empire]] under the command of Syagrius. He extended his rule across much of [[Gaul]], conquering the Alemanni and the [[Visigothic Kingdom|Visigothic kingdom]] of Aquitania. Clovis was baptized between 498 and 506, largely at the urging of his wife, Clotilde. His adoption of [[Catholic Church|Catholicism]], rather than the [[Arianism]] of most other Germanic tribes, led to widespread conversions among the Franks. [[Charles de Gaulle]] called him "the first king of what would become France."

[[Archaeological culture|Archaeological culture]] of the Paleoindian period in North America, dated to 13,050 to 12,750 years before present (BP). It is named after the type site at Blackwater Draw near Clovis, New Mexico, where stone tools were found alongside Columbian mammoth remains in 1929. Its most distinctive tools are Clovis points, large fluted projectile points sometimes exceeding 10 cm in length. Clovis groups were highly mobile [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]] who relied on big game, especially mammoths, and may have contributed to the [[Pleistocene|Late Pleistocene]] [[Megafauna|megafauna]] extinctions, though this is controversial. More than 20 caches of Clovis artifacts have been identified. The long-held "Clovis First" model, which treated Clovis as the earliest human presence in the Americas, is generally rejected because several sites, such as Monte Verde II, date at least a thousand years earlier.

Comic performer who uses physical [[Comedy|comedy]], usually in distinctive makeup and [[Costume|costume]]. The most ancient known clowns come from Egypt's Fifth Dynasty, around 2400 BC, when the roles of [[Priest|priest]] and clown were traditionally held by the same people. Many indigenous American cultures have ritual clowns; among the Lakota and Dakota, the Heyoka is a backward clown who does everything in reverse. The [[Circus|circus]] clown developed from comic roles in [[Theatre|theater]] and variety shows in the 19th to mid-20th centuries, with outlandish costumes, colorful wigs and exaggerated footwear. Joseph Grimaldi, an English pantomime actor, expanded the role in the early 1800s and created the whiteface makeup design used by many modern Western clowns.

Saltwater fish of the genus *Amphiprion*, also called anemonefish. Clownfish live in warm Indo-Pacific [[Coral reef|coral reefs]] and shelter among [[Sea anemone|sea anemones]], which protect them from predators. Groups consist of a breeding female and male with non-breeding individuals, ranked by size with the breeding female at the top. When the female disappears, the breeding male changes sex to take her place. The ocellaris clownfish is among the most commonly traded marine fish, and captures for the aquarium trade have contributed to population declines. Clownfish appear in the film *Finding Nemo* (2003).

[[Voluntary association|Association]] of people united by a common interest or goal. Clubs range from hobby, sport and social groups to charitable service, political and religious organizations. Clubs existed in all ancient states with detailed records, including [[Ancient Rome]], where they were known as collegia. Early English clubs were informal gatherings of friends for dining or drinking, and 17th-century coffee-house clubs had no permanent financial bond between members. In 1675 King Charles II issued a proclamation to suppress coffee houses, but withdrew it almost at once. [[Ben Jonson]] founded a club that met at the Devil Tavern in [[London]]. In the 18th and 19th centuries, some clubs became permanent institutions with fixed clubhouses. Clubs have faced criticism for historically reinforcing class, gender and ethnic barriers.

Short staff or stick, usually of [[Wood|wood]], used as a [[Weapon|weapon]] or tool. Clubs are also called cudgels, batons, truncheons, nightsticks and impact weapons, and most can be swung with one hand. Clubs have been wielded since prehistory; a conflict among [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherers]] at Nataruk in Turkana, [[Kenya]], about 10,000 years ago left blunt-force trauma. Until tasers and capsicum spray became available, [[Police|police]] forces relied on wooden clubs such as the truncheon, baton or lathi. The military mace is a more sophisticated descendant, with a metal head that may be spiked, knobbed or flanged. Clubs appear in [[Heraldry|heraldry]], where they often represent strength and authority, and on Spanish-suited playing cards.

Explosive weapon, air-dropped or ground-launched, that releases smaller submunitions over a wide area. Most are designed to kill personnel or destroy vehicles, though some target runways or power transmission lines. The German SD-2, nicknamed the Butterfly Bomb, was the first significantly used cluster bomb. Cluster munitions were used in [[World War II]] against both civilian and military targets, including Tokyo and [[Kyushu]]. They have been produced by 34 countries and used in at least 23. Unexploded bomblets can kill or maim civilians long after a conflict ends, with failure rates ranging from two percent to over 40 percent. The Convention on Cluster Munitions, adopted in [[Dublin]], Ireland, in May 2008, took effect on August 1, 2010; as of February 10, 2022, 123 states had joined it. The United States, Russia and China have not joined; they argue that the weapons remain militarily valuable, while humanitarian groups stress their remnant risks.

Mechanical device that connects or disconnects a rotating input shaft from an output shaft. In a [[Car|motor vehicle]], the clutch links the [[Engine|engine]] to the transmission, so that disengaging it decouples engine speed from the driven wheels. Most manual transmissions use dry clutches, in which a [[Friction|friction]] disc is pressed against the flywheel by a spring; wet clutches run in oil, which cools them and lengthens their life. Centrifugal clutches engage automatically as speed rises, as in [[Motorcycle|small motorcycles]] and [[Chainsaw|chainsaws]]. In an electric drill, the clutch lets the bit spin at motor speed, at a slower speed or not at all.

Phylum of over 11,000 species of mostly marine invertebrates, including [[Jellyfish|jellyfish]], [[Coral|corals]] and [[Sea anemone|sea anemones]]. Cnidarians are named for cnidocytes, specialized stinging cells with ejectable organelles used mainly to capture prey. Their gelatinous bodies have a simple nerve net and a single opening. Cnidarians mostly take one of two body forms, the sessile polyp or the swimming medusa. The four main classes are Anthozoa (sea anemones, corals and sea pens), Scyphozoa (true jellyfish), Cubozoa (box jellies) and Hydrozoa. Many scleractinian corals form the structural foundation of [[Coral reef|coral reefs]]. Fossils from the [[Ediacaran|Ediacaran period]], about 580 million years ago, show that the phylum is very ancient.

Danish king of England, Denmark and [[Norway]], also called Canute the Great. Cnut won the English throne in 1016, in the wake of centuries of Viking activity in northwestern Europe. He acceded to the Danish throne in 1018, uniting the crowns of England and Denmark, and claimed Norway in 1028. Historians call his combined realms the [[North Sea]] Empire. In 1031, [[Scotland|Malcolm II of Scotland]] submitted to him, though Anglo-Norse influence there did not last. Cnut enforced legal reforms, fostered [[Christianity|Christianity]] through church endowments, and made a pilgrimage to [[Rome]]. Medieval historian Norman Cantor called him "the most effective king in Anglo-Saxon history." His realms fragmented after his death amid succession disputes among his sons.

Land next to the sea, forming the boundary between land and the [[Ocean|ocean]]. Coasts are shaped by waves, [[Erosion|erosion]] and the composition of rock and soil. They support rich ecosystems, including [[Wetland|wetlands]], salt marshes and [[Mangrove|mangroves]] that provide nursery habitat for fish. Coastal ecosystems such as mangroves and seagrasses have a much higher capacity for carbon sequestration than many terrestrial ecosystems. Coastal flooding and saltwater intrusion are increasing with [[Climate change|climate change]] and [[Sea level|sea level]] rise. According to a United Nations atlas, about 44% of the human population lived within 150 km of the sea as of 2013. Fisheries, [[Aquaculture|aquaculture]] and [[Tourism|tourism]] are major coastal economic activities. Because coasts are constantly changing, their exact perimeter cannot be measured, a problem known as the coastline paradox.

Outer garment for the upper body, worn for warmth or fashion. Coats usually have long sleeves and close with [[Button|buttons]], [[Zipper|zippers]], hook-and-loop fasteners, toggles or a [[Belt (clothing)|belt]], and may have collars, shoulder straps or hoods. The word stems from Old French and Latin, and its modern meaning dates to c. 1300. Western-style coats may trace to the sleeved, front-fastened coats of Scythian nomads of the [[Eurasian Steppe]]. By the eighteenth century, overcoats had begun to replace capes and [[Cloak|cloaks]] as outerwear in Western fashion. After the [[Industrial Revolution]], cheaper cloth let people of lower social classes adopt the outdoor wear of the wealthy. The trench coat was developed during World War I for British officers as a waterproof overcoat.

Diurnal [[Mammal|mammal]] of the [[Raccoon|raccoon]] family, Procyonidae, native to the Americas. Coatis, also called coatimundis, range from the southwestern United States through South America. They are about the size of a large [[Cat|house cat]], with a long, ringed tail that they hold upright to keep groups together in tall vegetation. Females and young form bands of 4–40 individuals, while adult males are largely solitary outside the breeding season. Coatis are omnivorous, eating fruit, invertebrates and small vertebrates. The eastern mountain coati is classified as Endangered due to habitat loss in the Andes.

Hard, lustrous metal; [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with symbol Co and atomic number 27. Cobalt is ferromagnetic and is protected from oxidation by a passivating oxide film. It is used primarily in [[Lithium-ion battery|lithium-ion batteries]] and in magnetic, wear-resistant and high-strength [[Alloy|alloys]]. Cobalt-based blue pigments have been used since antiquity to color glass, paints and jewelry. Its name derives from an ore that 16th-century German silver miners considered a nuisance, possibly named after a goblin. Today cobalt is mostly produced as a by-product of [[Copper|copper]] and [[Nickel|nickel]] mining. In 2024, production exceeded 300,000 tons, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) accounting for more than 80%. Cobalt is the active center of cobalamins, also known as [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B12]], which is essential for all animals.

Cultivated shrub in the family Erythroxylaceae, native to western South America. Coca leaves contain the alkaloid [[Cocaine|cocaine]], which acts as a mild stimulant when chewed or brewed as tea. The plant was domesticated during the [[Holocene]], and coca leaves have been chewed in South America for at least 8,000 years. The Incas used coca in labor, religion and trade. Coca leaves are used commercially in teas, foods, cosmetics and beverages. A decocainized leaf extract is authorized for flavoring [[Coca-Cola]] in the United States.

Cola [[Soft drink|soft drink]] manufactured by [[The Coca-Cola Company]]. Pharmacist John Stith Pemberton invented it in 1886 in [[Atlanta]], initially marketing it as a temperance drink and patent medicine. In 1888 Asa Griggs Candler acquired the ownership rights, and his marketing led to the drink's global dominance. The name refers to [[Coca|coca]] leaves and kola nuts, a source of [[Caffeine|caffeine]]. The formula remains a trade secret. The company sells concentrate to licensed bottlers, and a typical 12 fl oz (355 mL) can contains 38 grams of sugar. In 2013, Coke products were sold in over 200 countries and territories.

Tropane alkaloid and [[Stimulant|central nervous system stimulant]] derived from the leaves of [[Coca|coca]] plants. Coca leaves are processed into cocaine paste and then converted to cocaine hydrochloride. Historically used as a topical local anesthetic, cocaine has been largely replaced by alternatives because of its abuse potential, adverse effects and cost. It acts as a [[Serotonin|serotonin]]–norepinephrine–[[Dopamine|dopamine]] reuptake inhibitor, producing euphoria and increased alertness. Acute use can cause [[Tachycardia|tachycardia]], [[Hypertension|hypertension]] and seizures, and overdose may lead to a [[Stroke|stroke]] or [[Myocardial infarction|heart attack]]. Chronic use may cause dependence, withdrawal and neurotoxicity. An estimated 20 million people used cocaine in 2019. Since 1961, the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs has required countries to make recreational use a crime.
